← Basement waterproofing bid calculator

How much to charge for basement waterproofing

The number a homeowner wants is a price per lineal foot of drain tile. That number is not a takeoff. An 80 lf finished basement with an existing sump is not the same job as a 55 lf seepage house with four window wells and a new pit. The footage is smaller on the seepage house. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count wells and the pit, not just lineal feet

Interior French drain is cut, haul, pipe, gravel, and pour-back. Exterior excavation is a different job — spoil, membrane, and a yard to put back. Crawl encapsulation prices floor vapor and wall liner, not drain footage. Gutter work prices eaves and downspouts. A retaining wall prices height and geogrid. Waterproofing prices water-entry points. Quoting all three from a published per-lineal-foot number is how the first window well eats the field margin.

A shorter basement can cost more

Each window well is typically a cover, a drain into the interior system, and a few hours that never appear in the perimeter tape. A new pit is excavation and a liner, not a swap on an existing crock. Battery backup and freeze-proof discharge are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 55 lf seepage house with four wells, a new pit, a battery backup, and 60 feet of freeze-protected discharge prices about $15,148 ($275 per lineal foot, 74 crew-hours). The same shop’s 80 lf finished basement with an existing 1/3 HP sump and 20 feet of discharge prices about $12,157 ($152 per lineal foot, 59 hours, walk-away $9,118). Matching the brochure job’s per-foot number on the seepage house is how that job becomes a loss.

Exterior excavation is not a markup on interior drain

Interior drain cuts a strip of slab. Exterior excavation opens the foundation, hauls spoil, and restores landscaping. On the sample rates a 100 lf exterior job prices about $26,206 ($262 per lineal foot, 207 crew-hours) — more than double the 80 lf interior brochure job, not because the wall is longer but because the dirt is. Treating that as a blended “add 30%” is how the yard-destroyer special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first dump ticket.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $36/h tech loaded at 32% payroll burden is $47.52. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not an engineering specification, a dry-basement warranty, a hydrostatic-pressure guarantee, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Water-entry diagnosis, pump sizing, and whether the discharge can freeze are yours to confirm.

Price your basement

Common questions

How much to charge for basement waterproofing?

Charge from perimeter lineal feet, wall height, window wells, crack repair, new versus existing sump, backup pump, discharge run, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 80 lf finished basement with an existing 1/3 HP sump and 20 feet of discharge prices around $12,157 on the sample rates in this calculator — about $152 per lineal foot.

Why is a per-lineal-foot waterproofing quote dangerous?

Homeowners measure the basement perimeter. Window wells, a new pit, battery backup, and freeze-proof discharge do not scale with that footage. Matching a cheaper per-foot quote written for a finished basement with an existing sump is how a seepage house becomes a two-day loss.

Does a shorter basement always cost less to waterproof?

No. On the sample rates a 55 lf seepage house with four window wells, a new pit, a battery backup, and 60 feet of freeze-protected discharge prices around $15,148 ($275 per lineal foot), while a longer 80 lf finished basement with an existing sump prices around $12,157 ($152 per lineal foot).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not waterproofing, construction, engineering, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a dry-basement warranty, or an engineering specification — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Common questions

      What does this waterproofing bid actually add up?

      The price adds up drain or excavation labor and material by system, a wall-membrane and floor-vapor-barrier area, concrete pour-back and spoil disposal, window wells and covers, floor-crack and wall-crack injection, a new sump pit when checked, a primary pump, a backup pump, discharge pipe and a freeze-proof kit when checked, and a dehumidifier when checked — plus travel and equipment, overhead, and your target margin, all from the perimeter, wall height, and system you enter, not a flat price-per-lineal-foot list.

      Why does an 80 lf basement with an existing sump price so differently from a 120 lf seepage house?

      Interior drain, exterior excavation, and crawl-space encapsulation each start from their own hours and material rates per lineal foot or per 100 sq ft of wall. On top of that, a new sump pit, a backup pump, extra window wells, crack injection, and freeze-proof discharge are all separate line items that do not scale with perimeter footage — a quote written for a brochure job with an existing pit and no wells prices a seepage house with four wells and a new pit the same way, which is exactly how that job loses money after the first well.

      Why do I set hours per 100 square feet of wall instead of per lineal foot for the membrane?

      Wall membrane and floor vapor barrier are area-based work — the wall area is perimeter times wall height, so a tall basement wall costs more to membrane than a short crawl-space wall of the same perimeter, even though both are priced from the same lineal footage of drain or excavation.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your lineal footage, wages, costs, or prices. Only your business details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser’s local storage so you do not retype them, and the customer’s details are never saved.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already includes your target margin on top of labor, materials, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — drain or excavation, membrane, wells, cracks, pit, pumps, and discharge — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all.

      Does this check hydrostatic pressure, drainage design, or structural conditions?

      No. Hours and material rates are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not an engineering specification, a dry-basement warranty, or a guarantee of hydrostatic performance. Whether a specific foundation needs interior drain versus exterior excavation, how deep a new sump pit should sit, or whether a wall crack is a moisture issue or a structural one is still a judgment call for the site walk — this tool prices the system you choose, it does not choose it for you.

      How is this different from a paid platform like Oblyss?

      Oblyss is a paid CRM and estimating platform built for foundation repair and waterproofing companies, with scheduling and warranty tracking across every job the company runs. This calculator connects to nothing: you price one job in your browser, with no account to make, cancel, or pay for. See this calculator vs. Oblyss for which job fits which situation.

      Why not just quote a flat rate per lineal foot like a lot of the trade does?

      A flat rate does not see window wells, whether the sump pit is new or existing, floor and wall crack injection, a backup pump, or freeze-proof discharge. A shorter perimeter with more of that scope can cost more than a longer, simpler one. See this calculator vs. a flat rate per lineal foot for a worked example.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-lineal-foot.html.text:
← Basement Waterproofing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per lineal foot

"$150 a lineal foot" is not a price for a waterproofing job — it is a price for one specific basement's wells, sump, cracks, backup, and discharge, quietly applied to every job that calls in.

What a flat rate per lineal foot is

A flat rate per lineal foot of perimeter is the fastest way to quote: multiply the wall length by a number and read off a price. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a homeowner holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one basement — one wall height, an existing sump, no window wells, no crack injection, no backup pump, a short discharge run — and then reused for every job afterward, whether or not the next basement looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the waterproofing system, perimeter and wall height, window wells, floor and wall crack injection, whether the sump is new or existing, the pump and backup pump, discharge run and whether it needs freeze protection, crew wage, material costs, and target margin. It prices wells, cracks, the pit, the backup, and discharge separately from wall and floor membrane, and returns a price above your target margin — for this basement, not a generic one.

What a flat rate per lineal foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/lf whether the basement has zero window wells and an existing sump or four wells and a brand-new pit. Prices window wells, and a new sump pit versus an existing one, as their own labor and material lines, so a well-heavy job never prices off the same number as a well-free one.
Prices "the perimeter" as one lineal-foot figure, with no separate line for floor or wall crack injection. Charges crack injection by count and length, so a job with 12 lf of floor cracks and two wall-crack injections costs more than one with none.
Has no line for a backup pump or a freeze-proof discharge run, regardless of how far north the basement is or how the homeowner wants to be protected. Prices the pump, backup pump, and discharge — including a freeze-proof kit — directly, so a job needing a battery backup and 60 feet of freeze-protected discharge costs more than one needing neither.
An 80 lf finished basement with an existing sump and a 55 lf seepage house with four wells, a new pit, a battery backup, and freeze-proof discharge get quoted off the same $/lf number — and the shorter, harder job would be quoted for less. The brochure job and the seepage house price on their own wells, cracks, sump, backup, and discharge — not on perimeter alone — so the shorter, harder job prices higher, correctly.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price and the price per lineal foot, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the contractor commits to it.

Two basements, the same wells-blind rate

Using this calculator's own verified defaults for its interior-drain system, wage, material, and overhead inputs:

JobFlat per-lineal-foot quoteScope-driven priceGap
80 lf finished basement, existing sump, no wells, no cracks (the brochure job)$151.97/lf × 80 lf = $12,157.31$12,157.31 (this is where the $151.97/lf rate comes from)—
55 lf seepage house: 4 window wells, new pit, battery backup, 60 lf freeze-proof discharge, 2 wall cracks, 12 lf floor cracks$151.97/lf × 55 lf = $8,358.15$15,147.73The flat rate undercharges by about $6,790 — about 81% too low.

Both rows use the same $151.97/lf rate, taken from the 80 lf brochure job itself — the most favorable possible flat rate for the comparison, not an inflated one. The seepage house has 25 fewer lineal feet of perimeter and still costs about 25% more to do correctly, because wells, the new pit, the backup pump, freeze-proof discharge, and crack injection do not scale with lineal feet. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see which side of the gap it falls on.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one basement it was built for, and nothing about a per-lineal-foot number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per lineal foot get a waterproofing quote wrong?

Because perimeter footage is not the cost driver. Window wells, a new sump pit versus an existing one, floor and wall crack injection, a battery or water-powered backup pump, and a freeze-proof discharge run all cost real crew hours and material that do not scale with lineal feet of perimeter. A shorter perimeter with more of that scope can cost more than a longer, simpler one.

What does a flat rate usually leave out entirely?

Window wells, sump and backup-pump work, crack injection, and discharge. A job with four window wells, a new pit, a battery backup, and 60 feet of freeze-protected discharge needs real labor and material for each of those, and a per-lineal-foot number has no line for any of them.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

In the worked example on this page, applying an 80 lf brochure job's own flat rate per lineal foot to a 55 lf seepage house undercharges that job by roughly 81% — using this calculator's own verified defaults, not a cherry-picked case.

Is a flat rate per lineal foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — similar wall height, an existing sump, no wells or crack injection, similar discharge — a flat rate can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know how much of that scope a given basement needs until it is actually measured.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the wage, material, and overhead numbers you enter and turns them into a price for the perimeter, wells, cracks, sump, backup, and discharge you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat rate per lineal foot is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the basement stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. Oblyss

Both end with a price you can hand a customer, built on opposite assumptions about what you are willing to install and pay for.

What Oblyss is

Oblyss is a paid CRM and estimating platform built specifically for foundation repair and waterproofing companies: pre-loaded product categories for structural repair, waterproofing, crawl space, and drainage work, plus scheduling, warranty tracking, and job costing across every job the company runs, on an ongoing subscription. It is built to run day-to-day operations for a company doing many jobs, not to price a single basement once.

Getting there means creating an account and paying an ongoing subscription priced by users and features.

What this calculator is

This page does not schedule anything and keeps no account. You open it in a browser, type wall length and height, window wells, crack injection, whether the sump is new or existing, backup pump, and discharge line, and it shows a price for that one job. Close the tab and it is gone unless you save a share link or print a proposal — there is no CRM, no warranty tracker, and no subscription.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want CRM, scheduling, and warranty tracking for every job my waterproofing company runs. Oblyss or a comparable paid platform — ongoing CRM and warranty tracking is exactly its job, and this calculator keeps no job history.
I have one basement to price right now and want a number before the bid goes out. This calculator — type the wall, drain, and sump details, get a price, no account.
I do not want to create an account or start a subscription to price a single job. This calculator — nothing to sign up for.
I want the tool to track warranty claims and remember every job I have bid over time. Oblyss or a comparable paid platform — this calculator has no job list and no memory between visits beyond what your own browser keeps.

Neither tool is the wrong choice in general. A waterproofing company running CRM, scheduling, and warranty claims across many jobs a season is the case a paid platform is built for. A single basement, priced once before the bid goes out, is the case this page is built for.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Oblyss?

They fit different points in the job. Oblyss is a paid CRM and estimating platform built for foundation repair and waterproofing companies: pre-loaded product categories, scheduling, warranty tracking, and job costing across every job a company runs, on an ongoing subscription. This page does one thing: you type wall length and height, window wells, crack injection, sump and discharge details into a browser, and it shows a price for that one job, right now, with no account and no subscription. If you want a platform that runs CRM and warranty tracking for an ongoing waterproofing business, that is what Oblyss is built for. If you want to price one basement before a bid goes out, this page does that with nothing to sign up for.

Is this page affiliated with Oblyss?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Oblyss. Oblyss is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

This page is a factual comparison of what each tool does, not an evaluation of which is better. Details about Oblyss above describe the general shape of the product as publicly described at the time of writing and may have changed — verify against Oblyss's own site before deciding.
